messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Non-profit Worker
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 70

Ms. Kapoor sits in the therapy office with her hands folded in her lap, a thin gold bangle sliding up and down her wrist as she speaks. She is sixty-seven, a lifelong resident of a mid-sized city where she works as a program coordinator for a local non-profit that supports immigrant families. Her husband of forty-three years, Raj, waits in the car during sessions—he drove her here, as she no longer takes the bus alone.

She tells the story in fragments, as if pulling splinters from deep skin. The assault happened twelve years ago, shortly after she and Raj had moved their aging parents into their home. One afternoon, while Raj was at work and her mother-in-law napped upstairs, a man came to the door posing as a utility inspector. She let him in. He was polite at first, then he closed the door behind him. She remembers the smell of his cologne—sandalwood and something bitter—and the way her mother-in-law’s clock radio played old film songs from the other room while it happened.

For years she told no one. She scrubbed the kitchen floor that evening until her knuckles bled, then cooked dinner as usual. In South Asian communities, she explains, “these things are not spoken of. You are the one who brings shame.” So she buried it. She continued her work at the non-profit, helping other women fill out paperwork for housing and food stamps, never once mentioning her own need.

The symptoms crept in slowly, then all at once. Two years ago, her non-profit began a new program for survivors of domestic violence. Ms. Kapoor volunteered to manage intake calls. She thought she could help. But the first time a client described being trapped in a room by her partner, Ms. Kapoor felt her chest clamp shut. She excused herself, walked to the bathroom, and stood gripping the sink while images flickered behind her eyes—the man’s hands, the clock radio, the weight of her own silence. She stopped taking those calls. Now she works only on data entry, sitting in a back office with the door closed, flinching when colleagues knock.

At home, she cannot bear the sound of a doorbell. She has asked Raj to put a sign on the front door: “No solicitors.” When the television shows any scene with a sudden male intrusion, she leaves the room without explanation. Her sleep is broken; she wakes at 3 a.m. most nights, heart pounding, convinced she hears footsteps on the porch. She checks the locks three times before bed, then again at midnight, then again at two.

She has withdrawn from the temple group she attended for decades. The chanting, she says, used to soothe her. Now the close bodies and the scent of incense—something about that sandalwood—makes her dizzy. Her daughter, who lives two states away, calls every Sunday. Ms. Kapoor keeps the conversations short. She cannot tell her why. She cannot tell anyone. The shame has calcified into a second skeleton.

Recently, she started crying during a routine visit to the grocery store. A man in a blue cap—the same kind the attacker wore—stood near the produce aisle. She abandoned her cart and walked home in the rain, soaking her sari. Raj found her on the porch, shivering, unable to explain.

The PCL-5 score of 70 reflects what she will not say outright: that she replays the assault every day, that she feels dead inside, that she has started wishing she had never opened the door. She looks at her hands while she speaks, the gold bangle catching the light. She does not look at the therapist. She is waiting, perhaps, for judgment. Or for permission to feel what she has spent twelve years trying not to feel.
